extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Kant, philosophy of mathematics, and history of philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Survey and explanatory account of Kant's views on mathematical judgment, concept-construction, the role of intuition, and the place of mathematics within Transcendental Idealism. Summarizes Kant's pre-critical and critical positions and major interpretive debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of mathematical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: "to construct a concept means to exhibit a priori the intuition corresponding to it" (A713/B741).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant's central claim: mathematical cognition derives from construction — e.g., a triangle is constructed by exhibiting a singular intuition that corresponds to the concept <triangle>. From such a singular a priori display one can derive universal truths because particular determinations are 'entirely indifferent' to the concept. Discussions concern how an intuition adequately displays a concept and the role of imagination and construction in proofs (examples: geometric constructions, ostensive vs symbolic construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only magnitudes are constructible in pure intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant: "only the concept of magnitudes" (quantities) can be constructed in pure intuition, since "qualities cannot be exhibited in anything but empirical intuition" (A714/B742).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to a principled distinction between mathematics (concerned with quantities that can be intuited) and philosophy (concerned with qualities). This underpins why arithmetic and geometry are paradigmatic mathematical domains and frames debates about arithmetic, algebraic magnitudes, and the role of space and time as pure intuitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical judgments are synthetic a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's claim that mathematical judgments are both synthetic and a priori (e.g., arithmetic '7 + 5 = 12' cannot be found in the concepts alone and requires intuition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues necessity (a priori) and ampliative content (synthetic) via examples in arithmetic and Euclidean geometry. Debates follow about whether axioms only or also mathematical inference is synthetic, and whether intuition supplies evidence for axioms, inferences, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of mathematical method via construction and intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice proceeds by a "chain of inferences that is always guided by intuition" and so differs from philosophical analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant contrasts synthesis (mathematics) with analysis (philosophy). Pre-critical statements emphasize geometers' reliance on synthesis and sensible signs; critical account develops a technical notion of construction in pure intuition. This criterion explains why mathematical method cannot be straightforwardly applied to metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure intuition (space and time) grounds mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts must be exhibited in pure intuition (space and time as forms of sensibility), which explains the possibility of synthetic a priori mathematical judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that only space and time can provide the pure intuitions required for construction; Prolegomena and Critique give complementary arguments (analytic vs synthetic method). This underlies the applicability of mathematics to appearances and grounds the Axioms of Intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical reasoning limited to formal objects given a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical reasoning is necessarily directed at objects "determinately given in pure intuition a priori and without any empirical data" (A724/B752).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, mathematics properly concerns formal spatial/temporal magnitudes; while its results apply to empirical appearances, mathematical method cannot replace philosophical or empirical inquiry into materially given content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ostensive vs symbolic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between ostensive construction (displaying spatial figures) and symbolic construction (concatenating arithmetic/algebraic symbols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ostensive construction is characteristic of geometric practice; symbolic construction covers arithmetic/algebraic operations. Kant uses this to explain how different mathematical disciplines instantiate the general thesis of construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of diagrams/intuitions in geometric proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric proofs involve an indispensable diagrammatic role for intuitions; intuitions exhibit relations used in proofs and infer universal rules from singular displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drawing a pair of intersecting chords in a circle and inferring the universal relation; debates exist whether such intuitions function phenomenologically (immediacy) or logically (singularity/instantiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical principles drawn from intuition, not from pure understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical principles proper are "drawn only from intuition" and are not part of the system of principles of pure understanding, though Axioms of Intuition provide a meta-principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant locates mathematical principles in intuition while the Axioms of Intuition (e.g., 'All intuitions are extensive magnitudes') explain why mathematical principles apply to appearances. This distinction motivates interpretive issues about scope and foundations of mathematical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms of Intuition — All intuitions are extensive magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's Axioms of Intuition state that 'All intuitions are extensive magnitudes' (A161/B202).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreters read this as a meta-principle explaining why mathematical principles (about space and time) are applicable to appearances: both pure and empirical intuitions are extensive magnitudes subject to mathematical determination. Alternative readings exist in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schematism and mediation between concepts and intuitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories must be 'schematized'—transcendental schemata mediate between pure concepts of the understanding and sensible intuitions; mathematical concepts are special as pure yet sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions arise whether mathematical concepts require a distinguishable schematum and how the transcendental imagination operates in mathematical contexts (e.g., number as schema of magnitude). This concerns the internal mechanics of how concepts apply to intuitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic vs synthetic methods for explaining possibility of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Two argumentative strategies: analytic method traces cognition to its mental origin; synthetic method derives cognition from explicated cognitive sources (Prolegomena vs Critique uses respectively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant employs both methods at different points: the Prolegomena argues from mathematical judgments to forms of sensibility; the Critique derives mathematical judgments from the forms of sensibility. This methodological distinction structures Kant's answers to 'How is pure mathematics possible?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for intuition as non-conceptual representation: immediacy vs singularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive debate: Parsons emphasizes immediacy/phenomenological presence of mathematical intuition; Hintikka emphasizes singularity (intuitions as singular terms/instantiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These competing criteria shape different readings of Kant's account of intuition's role in grounding synthetic judgments. The debate affects whether intuition is taken as perceptual immediacy or as logical singular instantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical definitions, axioms, and demonstrations provide special certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics attains a 'thorough grounding' in definitions, axioms, and demonstrations that Kant claims cannot be 'achieved or imitated' by philosophy or the physical sciences (A727/B755).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard explains why Kant treats mathematics as paradigm of evidence and certainty; it motivates analysis of what aspects of mathematical rigor are transferable to other disciplines and what is unique to mathematical construction.
